info.bio: Buzzcocks es una banda de punk rock británico, cuya combinación de energía instrumental, agresividad rítmica, cinismo lírico y querencia por la buena melodía pop colocaron a los Buzzcocks como uno de los primeros combos punk-pop de la historia (junto a los Ramones). Fueron influenciados tanto por los Sex Pistols como por Velvet Underground, los Who, Stooges, Troggs (a quienes versionaron “I can’t control myself”) o el garage y el beat de los años 60.

scenes.name: Punk rock (1976-77)
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El «Año Cero»: hacia el verano de 1977 el punk ya era una parodia de sí mismo y su frágil alianza entre chicos obreros y bohemios de escuela de arte se rompe. De un lado quedan los «punks verdaderos», populistas, que desembocarán en el Oi! y el hardcore; del otro, la vanguardia que se llamará postpunk, que vio en 1977 no un retorno al rock crudo sino la ocasión de romper con la tradición. Su legado común: la fe en el poder de la música y el «hazlo tú mismo».
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: Do it yourself
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Spiral Scratch de los Buzzcocks (New Hormones, enero de 1977) fue la primera declaración polémica de independencia: autoeditado, con los detalles de grabación en la contratapa y un número de catálogo que era un chiste reichiano (ORG-1). The Desperate Bicycles («It was easy, it was cheap — go and do it»; «Smokescreen» costó 153 libras) catalizaron una legión: Swell Maps, Scritti Politti, Young Marble Giants, Television Personalities, Thomas Leer, Daniel Miller. Swell Maps y TVP inventan una rama que hace de la ingenuidad un fetiche: voces débiles, ritmos temblorosos y guitarras frenéticas. El riesgo: pasar de «cualquiera puede hacerlo» al mandato de sonar como si cualquiera pudiera.

scenes.name: Punk-rock británico
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La gira de los Ramones de 1976 contagia a Inglaterra, donde el punk es combinación de moda y paro: la Gran Bretaña de Thatcher, con las ciudades industriales devastadas, convierte el «punk» en algo mucho más serio que lo que pretendían los Ramones. Malcolm McLaren inventa el sonido (Sex Pistols, «los Ramones con heroína y valium») y la imagen. The Clash, los más intelectuales (London Calling, Sandinista); Damned, Generation X, Buzzcocks (inventores del punk-pop), Vibrators. En Australia, Radio Birdman y los Saints. La segunda ola (GBH, UK Subs, Neurotics, New Model Army, Stiff Little Fingers) y el punk anarquista (Crass, Discharge, Rudimentari Peni, Subhumans).
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

podcast.title: Formation and Early Promotion (1975)
podcast.body: The Buzzcocks were formed sometime in 1975. Principals Howard Devoto and Pete Shelley promoted the Sex Pistols' first gig in Manchester at the Lesser Free Trade Hall, an event central to British punk rock culture and depicted in the movie "24 Hour Party People." "Anyway, that show was promoted by Howard Devoto and Pete Shelley, the two principals in The Buzzcocks."

podcast.body: Future members of the Buzzcocks were among the small audience of fewer than 50 people who attended the Sex Pistols' pivotal, though financially unsuccessful, gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4, 1976. This event served as a significant inspiration for them to pursue punk rock. "In the audience that night were future members of the buscocks and the pet shop boys and joy division and new order."

podcast.title: Establishing New Hormones Label
podcast.body: Energized by the Sex Pistols show and facing a music scene where no labels were interested in releasing their kind of music, the Buzzcocks established their own label, New Hormones. This act demonstrated that inexperienced musicians from a "musical backwater" like Manchester could successfully release their own records. "But with the scene being so new, there were no labels interested in releasing this kind of music, so they established their own label."

podcast.title: Peele Sessions Recordings (70s, 80s, 90s)
podcast.body: The Buzzcocks (referred to as "the Bus Cox") were part of the hundreds of bands that recorded "Peele Sessions" live at the BBC throughout the 70s, 80s, and 90s. These sessions, curated by DJ John Peel, played a vital role in showcasing new music while navigating the BBC's "Needle Time" regulations. "The Smiths, R.E.M., New Order, the Fall, Equivalent of the Buntyman, Susie the Banshee, the Bus Cox, the list is almost endless."

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Manchester Show
podcast.body: The Buzzcocks arranged for a still-unknown band, The Sex Pistols, to play the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4th, 1976. This gig became mythical and legendary, inspiring about 40 attendees to form bands like Joy Division, Pet Shop Boys, Simply Red, and The Smiths, and to establish Factory Records. "They arranged for a still unknown band called The Sex Pistols to play the lesser free trade hall in Manchester on June 4th, 1976, a show that has gone down in myth and legend as one of the most important gigs in the history of rock."

podcast.body: Even as a punk band from Manchester, the Buzzcocks were recognized for having a noticeable "groove" and elements of "soul music" in their sound, highlighting Manchester's pervasive connection to soul influences across genres. "Even Manchester punk bands, like listen to some buscox stuff they've got, you know, groove. They've got soul music, and soul music, but I mean, it's been really important in Manchester, and I don't know why, it has nothing in Liverpool."

xref.title: Debut at 100 Club (1976)
xref.body: This new group made its debut at the 100 Club Punk Rock Festival on September 20, 1976. On the first night, their drummer savagely beat up a well-known music journalist, and on the second night, the same individual was arrested for throwing a beer glass, blinding a girl in one eye. This drummer was Sid Vicious, who would later join the Sex Pistols. "The lineup featured a new group called The Clash, a group making their debut called Susie in the Band Sheets, the Buzzcocks were there around a few others."

xref.title: Lesser Free Trade Hall Gig (1976)
xref.body: On Friday, June 4, 1976, just after 7:30 PM, the Sex Pistols played a pivotal gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester. Despite selling tickets for only 50 pence, fewer than 50 people attended, making it a "failed money losing gig." Nonetheless, this concert proved to be a transformative moment for English rock, as the small audience included future members of influential bands such as the Buzzcocks, Pet Shop Boys, Joy Division, and New Order. "Didn't seem like much of the time, but this failed money losing gig became a turning point for English rock."

xref.title: Family Background and Early Influences
xref.body: Born in 1969, Jacob Dylan is the son of Bob Dylan and his model wife Sarah Dylan, who were married secretly in November 1965. Sarah inspired lyrics for many of Bob Dylan's songs before their 1977 divorce. Despite his father being a famous folk singer, Jacob preferred punk bands like The Clash, The Buzzcocks, and The Jam in his youth, and later had an aborted attempt at design school in New York. "Jacob Dylan is the son of Bob and his model wife Sarah Dylan. They were married in secret in November 1965. And for the next dozen years, she inspired the lyrics for a number of Dylan songs. Then they divorced in 1977. But before then, Jacob came along. That was 1969. And although he was the son of the world's most famous folk singer, he preferred punk bands like the clash and the buzz cocks as well as the jam."

xref.title: Formation and Early Influences
xref.body: The band was formed in Manchester in 1976 by Pete Shelley and Howard Devoto, who were both fans of The Velvet Underground and becoming interested in punk music. "The Buzzcocks were formed in Manchester in 1976 by two guys, Pete Shelley and Howard Devoto. Both were big velvet underground fans and had started paying more attention to this thing that people were calling punk."

xref.body: The Buzzcocks were one of the groups, along with The Fall and Joy Division, that began to "shake things up" in Manchester during the original punk era, contributing significantly to the city's cultural transformation from an industrial hub to a vibrant music scene. "Groups like the bus cocks in the fall and joy division had begun to shake things after in the original punk era."

xref.title: Manchester Punk Pioneer
xref.body: The Buzzcocks originated from Manchester and were recognized as one of the city's original punk bands, pioneering the expert blend of punk energy with pop melodies. "one of Manchester's original punk bands."

xref.title: New Wave Powerpop with Punk Influence
xref.body: The Buzzcocks are cited as a band that incorporated elements of punk into the new wave brand of Powerpop. Their sound, along with contemporaries like Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson, helped define the integration of Powerpop into the alternative rock world. "We had the cars, the shoes, the records, the buzz cocks, Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson."

xref.title: New Wave Powerpop with Punk Influence
xref.body: Elvis Costello is identified as an artist who brought a "little punk into the mix" of the new wave brand of Powerpop, alongside Joe Jackson and The Buzzcocks. He also had some of Nick Lowe's tracks turned into hits. "Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson. They brought a little punk into the mix."

xref.title: Origins from Sex Pistols Promotion
xref.body: The Buzzcocks initially formed when a couple of individuals in Manchester began promoting Sex Pistols shows, leading to their own band's inception. "The buzz cocks began as a couple of guys promoting sex pistols shows in Manchester."

xref.title: Peele Sessions Recordings (70s, 80s, 90s)
xref.body: The Buzzcocks (referred to as "the Bus Cox") were part of the hundreds of bands that recorded "Peele Sessions" live at the BBC throughout the 70s, 80s, and 90s. These sessions, curated by DJ John Peel, played a vital role in showcasing new music while navigating the BBC's "Needle Time" regulations. "The Smiths, R.E.M., New Order, the Fall, Equivalent of the Buntyman, Susie the Banshee, the Bus Cox, the list is almost endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

xref.title: Sex Pistols Manchester Show
xref.body: The Buzzcocks arranged for a still-unknown band, The Sex Pistols, to play the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4th, 1976. This gig became mythical and legendary, inspiring about 40 attendees to form bands like Joy Division, Pet Shop Boys, Simply Red, and The Smiths, and to establish Factory Records. "They arranged for a still unknown band called The Sex Pistols to play the lesser free trade hall in Manchester on June 4th, 1976, a show that has gone down in myth and legend as one of the most important gigs in the history of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

xref.title: Soulful Groove in Punk
xref.body: Even as a punk band from Manchester, the Buzzcocks were recognized for having a noticeable "groove" and elements of "soul music" in their sound, highlighting Manchester's pervasive connection to soul influences across genres. "Even Manchester punk bands, like listen to some buscox stuff they've got, you know, groove. They've got soul music, and soul music, but I mean, it's been really important in Manchester, and I don't know why, it has nothing in Liverpool."

xref.title: Unique Backstage Demand
xref.body: The Buzzcocks were the only band in Warped Tour history known to have made a specific backstage demand, requesting a bottle of champagne. "The buzz cocks, who were the only band to ever demand something backstage, they wanted a bottle of champagne."
